related_questions.question: At what stage of cancer is radiotherapy used?

text_blocks.snippet: Radiotherapy can be used at various stages of cancer, from early to advanced stages. It's not tied to a specific stage, but rather depends on the type of cancer, its location, and whether it has spread. Radiotherapy can be used to try to cure cancer, make other treatments more effective, or to relieve symptoms.

list.title: Neoadjuvant Therapy:
list.snippet: Radiotherapy can be given before surgery to shrink the tumor, making it easier to remove.

list.title: Adjuvant Therapy:
list.snippet: After surgery, radiotherapy can be used to kill any remaining cancer cells and prevent recurrence.

list.title: Primary Treatment:
list.snippet: In some cases, radiotherapy can be the primary treatment, especially when surgery is not an option or for early-stage cancers where it's highly effective.

list.title: Palliative Care:
list.snippet: In advanced cancer, radiotherapy can be used to relieve symptoms like pain, bleeding, or blockages caused by the cancer, even if it has spread to other parts of the body.

list.title: Targeted Areas:
list.snippet: Radiotherapy can be used to target specific areas where cancer has spread, such as bones, brain, or liver, to control symptoms and improve quality of life.

list.title: Chemoradiation:
list.snippet: In some cases, radiotherapy is combined with chemotherapy, either before, during, or after the radiotherapy course, to enhance its effectiveness.

list.title: Breast Cancer:
list.snippet: Radiotherapy is often used after breast-conserving surgery or a mastectomy, especially if the cancer is large or has spread to lymph nodes.

list.title: Lung Cancer:
list.snippet: Radiotherapy can be used for both early-stage lung cancers (including cases where surgery isn't an option) and for managing symptoms in advanced lung cancer.

list.title: Prostate Cancer:
list.snippet: Radiotherapy can be used to try to cure prostate cancer, treat it after it has grown outside the prostate, or to relieve bone pain if it has spread.

list.title: Colorectal Cancer:
list.snippet: Radiotherapy is less common for colon cancer, but may be used before or after surgery or to relieve symptoms if the cancer has spread.

related_questions.question: How long does a radiation therapy treatment take?
related_questions.snippet: The treatment itself is painless and takes only a few minutes. Each session lasts 15 to 30 minutes because of the time it takes to set up the equipment and put you in the right position. Before starting radiation therapy, you will have a simulation or planning scan to pinpoint the exact treatment area.
related_questions.title: Getting External Beam Radiation Therapy

text_blocks.snippet: Radiation therapy, or radiotherapy, is a cancer treatment that uses high-energy beams to damage and destroy cancer cells. It works by damaging the DNA within cancer cells, preventing them from dividing and growing. The process generally involves a consultation, simulation, treatment planning, and the actual delivery of radiation, which can be external or internal.
snippet_highlighted_words: a consultation, simulation, treatment planning, and the actual delivery of radiation

text_blocks.snippet: 1. Initial Consultation: A radiation oncologist reviews the patient's medical history, scans, and pathology reports, and performs a physical examination.
2. Simulation: This step involves using imaging techniques like X-rays or CT scans to pinpoint the exact location and shape of the tumor, creating a treatment field.

3. Treatment Planning: The radiation oncologist, along with a physicist and dosimetrist, designs the radiation treatment plan, optimizing the beam delivery to target the tumor while minimizing harm to surrounding healthy tissues.

list.title: External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT):
list.snippet: A machine (like a linear accelerator) directs high-energy beams from outside the body to the tumor. The patient lies on a table, and the machine moves around them, delivering radiation from different angles.

list.title: Internal Radiation Therapy (Brachytherapy):
list.snippet: A radiation source (solid or liquid) is placed inside the body, either temporarily or permanently, near the tumor.

text_blocks.snippet: 5. Monitoring: Throughout the treatment, the radiation oncologist and the team closely monitor the patient's response to therapy and adjust the treatment plan as needed.
6. Side Effects Management: Radiation therapy can cause side effects, and the medical team provides guidance and support to manage them.
